fig1_turbine_power.svg: Steady state is the assumption that makes control-volume problems tractable: nothing accumulates, so $dm_{cv}/dt$ and $dE_{cv}/dt$ both vanish (steady_mass_residual, is_steady) and the energy rate balance collapses to $\dot W=\dot m(h_1-h_2)$ for an adiabatic turbine with negligible KE and PE (turbine_power_adiabatic). The result is linear in both factors — 12 kg/s through an 800 kJ/kg drop is 9.6 MW. power_rate_steady and heat_rate_steady solve the same balance for the other unknowns.
fig2_when_ke_matters.svg: The standard phrase 'kinetic energy changes are negligible', made into a criterion. delta_ke returns $(V_2^2-V_1^2)/2$ in kJ/kg, so against a representative 1000 kJ/kg turbine enthalpy drop the kinetic term reaches 1% only near 141 m/s and 10% near 447 m/s. Turbine and compressor ducts run well below the first mark, so the term is dropped without apology; nozzles and diffusers exist precisely to push past the second, and there it is the enthalpy change that serves the kinetic one.
